Article Title: Microsoft is hiring a legal engineer to teach lawyers across the company how to…
Article Text:
Microsoft wants a lawyer who can build AI agents, and it is paying up to $278,900 for one

Why Microsoft wants a lawyer who can also write software

The legal engineer job is spreading from startups to Big Tech

Microsoft has spent the past two years telling everyone else that AI is about to change how work gets done. Now it wants someone to prove the point inside its own legal department. The company has posted a job for a principal legal engineer, an unusual hybrid role that asks for a practising attorney who can also ship software, with base pay topping out at $278,900 a year.The listing, spotted on LinkedIn this week by Business Insider, puts the hire inside Microsoft's Customer & Partner Solutions group, the arm that supports the company's commercial business. The work is deliberately hands-on: building AI agents, sharpening prompts, and training attorneys and paralegals to actually use the tools. "This is a role for a builder," Microsoft wrote in the job description, adding that the person will partner directly with engineering rather than advise from the sidelines. Microsoft did not respond to Business Insider's request for comment.Lawyers were the corporate world's great tech holdouts for decades, understandably nervous about tools that could get one detail wrong in a 90-page agreement. That resistance is thinning. Clients are now pushing outside firms toward tools like Harvey and Claude for Legal to turn work around faster and bill less for it.The same pressure has moved in-house. Legal teams are betting that software can handle contract edits and policy drafting, letting them keep more of the early work and hand outside counsel matters that are already halfway done.Microsoft has a head start here because it builds some of these tools itself. Its lawyers already use Copilot for routine work, including contract review, where it compares a draft against similar agreements, flags issues and suggests edits that match company policy. Harvey is being rolled out across Corporate, External, and Legal Affairs.Until recently, legal engineer was mostly a startup title, filled by ex-lawyers with technical chops who sat close to customers. Palantir posted its own embedded legal engineer role last month, promising to turn manual workflows into automated ones.Microsoft wants a law degree and at least seven years of practice. Experience with Harvey or Copilot is preferred. Base pay starts at $147,000.
Article Summary: Microsoft has posted a job for a principal legal engineer, an unusual hybrid role. It asks for a practising attorney who can also ship software, with base pay topping out at $278,900. The work is deliberately hands-on: building AI agents, sharpening prompts, and training attorneys.

Article Title: Apple Beats 360 headphones leak with new design, six colours and $299 price
Article Text:
Beats 360 to get a new design

Beats 360 may be offered in six colours

Beats 360 price and features

Apple’s unreleased Beats 360 over-ear headphones have allegedly appeared on several retail websites, revealing details about their design, colours, features and pricing ahead of an official launch. Listings for the headphones were spotted on Amazon U.K. and other retail websites before being removed. The leak suggests that the Beats 360 will have a new design compared with the current Beats Studio Pro and Solo 4. The headphones are expected to offer active noise cancellation, all-day battery life, IPX4 water and sweat resistance and support for both Apple and Android devices. Retail listings have also revealed a $299 US price.The leaked images show the Beats 360 with a different design from the company's existing over-ear headphones. The headphones feature a separate padded section underneath the headband, while the earcups have a more open mesh design.The padded section can reportedly be removed, as can the ear cushions. Retail listings also mention an Extra Cushion Kit, with Performance Knit and UltraPlush options. The leaked headphones also appear to be the same model that football player Lamine Yamal was seen wearing in Instagram posts earlier this summer.The Beats 360 is expected to launch in Sky, Black, Navy, Cloud, Pink and Volt. The six colour options would give the headphones a wider range of finishes than the current Beats Studio Pro and Solo 4.The Volt version has a bright neon-yellow finish.Retail listings have also revealed pricing. One listing showed the headphones at $299, while another listed them at £331.99. The Beats 360 is expected to feature active noise cancellation, with one product description claiming up to 1.75 times more noise cancellation than the Beats Studio Pro.The headphones reportedly do not use Apple's H2 chip or another Apple chip. They will, however, work with both Apple and Android devices. The headphones were also listed with an IPX4 rating for water and sweat resistance.The leaked product information claims the Beats 360 can offer all-day battery life even with ANC turned on. The headphones are said to fold flat and are expected to come with a woven ripstop fabric carrying case.
Article Summary: Listings for the headphones were spotted on Amazon U.K. and other retail websites. The leak suggests that the Beats 360 will have a new design compared with the current Beats Studio Pro and Solo 4. The headphones are expected to offer active noise cancellation, all-day battery life, IPX4 water and sweat resistance and support for both Apple and Android devices.

Article Title: ChatGPT can now send texts for Mac users with new Apple Messages plug-in, but why they need to be careful about using this feature
Article Text:
What the new ChatGPT feature actually does

Why this could be a sensitive move for Apple

How OpenAI says it's handling privacy

What users actually have to enable

OpenAI has rolled out a new Apple Messages plug-in for its popular chatbot ChatGPT on Mac, enabling the AI system to read, write and send texts directly through iMessage. The integration also allows ChatGPT to search conversations and generate summaries, expanding its functionality beyond productivity apps like Notes and Xcode. OpenAI stressed that the feature requires explicit user consent and runs locally on the Mac, using AppleScript and Accessibility tools to interact with the Messages app. During setup, users encounter multiple opt‑in menus, including a permissions screen confirming that on‑device message history will be accessed.The new ChatGPT plug-in introduced by OpenAI will enable the chatbot to conduct direct actions within the Apple Messages app. ChatGPT will be able to read, wrote and also send text messages on the behalf of the user. Along with this, it will also be able to search through the existing messages and create summaries or also pull other information out of conversations, effectively giving ChatGPT hands-on access to a core piece of Apple's messaging ecosystem.According to a report by Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman, Apple has built much of its brand identity around strong privacy protections, and the company has historically been especially protective of the contents of users' messages.A tool built by a third-party AI company, one capable of processing Apple customers' message data through OpenAI's own systems, is the kind of feature likely to draw scrutiny from privacy advocates and, potentially, from Apple itself. An Apple representative did not immediately respond to a request for comment on the launch.The timing adds another layer of tension: the feature arrives amid an already strained relationship between the two companies. Apple sued OpenAI last month, accusing the AI firm of stealing information related to upcoming Apple products.In response to questions about the new integration, OpenAI emphasised that the feature requires explicit user consent and does not build an index of a person's entire message history. The company said the plug-in runs locally on the Mac itself, relying on existing macOS tools such as AppleScript and Accessibility features to interact with the Messages app, rather than routing message data through a separate indexing system.Setting up the integration isn't a single toggle. When a user first configures it, ChatGPT displays a permissions screen explaining that the app will access the computer's on-device message history. Beyond that in-app consent step, users also need to adjust several privacy settings directly within the Mac's System Settings app, including enabling a feature called Full Disk Access. Users must additionally grant ChatGPT permission to access contact names and automation tools, a setup process similar to what's required to enable other AI-based automation software, such as Codex Computer Use.This isn't OpenAI's first foray into pulling personal data from Apple's ecosystem. The company recently added support for analyzing data from a user's iPhone or iPad Health app as well, though Apple's iOS and iPadOS include a built-in permission step specifically requiring users to approve sharing that health data with ChatGPT before it can proceed.
Article Summary: OpenAI has rolled out a new Apple Messages plug-in for its chatbot ChatGPT on Mac. The feature will enable the AI system to read, write and send texts directly through iMessage. The integration also allows the chatbot to search conversations and generate summaries. OpenAI stressed that the feature requires explicit user consent.

Article Title: Netflix unveils ‘VOID’, an AI model that can change a movie plot
Article Text:
Netflix

How Netflix VOID works







Netflix has unveiled an AI model that can alter the scene. While this is nothing new, Netflix’s model not just remove objects from video, it understands what should happen next, essentially altering the causality. Most object-removal technology leaves a gap where something used to be and/ or fills it with a plausible-looking background. VOID goes a step further: after erasing an object from a scene, it calculates how the surrounding environment should realistically respond to its absence, and in the process it adjusts the behaviour of other elements in the frame accordingly.The model, called VOID, is a vision-language system designed to edit video footage with a level of contextual awareness that sets it apart from several existing tools.For example, imagine this scenario: A movie director has just wrapped up a multi-million dollar action sequence where the star drives straight into a fiery, head-on collision. The cars explode, debris scatters, and the scene is a wrap.But suddenly, there is request to change the scene: The character survives and drive off into the sunset instead. This would mean costly reshoots or millions spent on computer-generated graphics.Netflix’s VOID can alter the scene and digitally erase the collision, the second vehicle, the smoke, and the flying debris. It will then generate new, realistic footage of pristine pavement, making it look as though the main character simply drove down an empty, peaceful road.The AI’s ‘magic’ lies in its grasp of real-world physics. Let us understand this by a different example. If a video shows a person jumping into a pool and splashing water onto the deck, VOID can completely erase the person. It will then intelligently alter the water and the wet concrete, leaving behind a perfectly still, undisturbed pool as if nobody had ever jumped in.“To train the model, we generate a new paired dataset of counterfactual object removals using Kubric and HUMOTO, where removing an object requires altering downstream physical interactions. During inference, a vision-language model identifies regions of the scene affected by the removed object. These regions are then used to guide a video diffusion model that generates physically consistent counterfactual outcomes,” Netflix said.“Experiments on both synthetic and real data show that our approach better preserves consistent scene dynamics after object removal compared to prior video object removal methods,” the company added.Netflix isn’t keeping this powerful tool locked behind studio doors, and made the VOID model available to the public on the AI platform Hugging Face, allowing anyone to download and use it.While there are already several video-altering tools on the market, such as Runway, DiffuEraser, and ProPainter, the Netflix team claims VOID is vastly superior, as per The Register.
Article Summary: Netflix has unveiled an AI model that can alter the scene. While this is nothing new, Netflix’s model not just remove objects from video, it understands what should happen next, essentially altering the causality. The model, called VOID, is a vision-language system designed to edit video footage with a level of contextual awareness.

Article Title: Fraudster uses Raigad SP’s WhatsApp display photo to dupe police staff, seeks Rs 50,000
Article Text:
A cyber fraudster impersonated Raigad SP on WhatsApp, targeting police personnel for money transfers, but the scam attempt was foiled. (AI-generated image)





NAVI MUMBAI: Raigad Cyber Police have registered a case against an unidentified fraudster who allegedly used the WhatsApp Display Picture (DP) of Raigad Superintendent of Police (SP) Anchal Dalal to deceive several police personnel into transferring money.On Thursday, the fraudster sent a message to Raigad SP's reader, PSI Siddheshwar Murkute, asking him to transfer money urgently. Murkute immediately realised that it was a modus operandi commonly used by cyber scammers, as the WhatsApp message was sent from an international number that was not saved in his mobile phone.Thereafter, PSI Murkute learnt that the same scammer had sent similar messages to several Raigad police personnel. Fortunately, no one fell prey to the fraud, as the police personnel were aware of this modus operandi used by cyber fraudsters.Subsequently, PSI Murkute registered an FIR against the unidentified accused under the relevant section of the BNS for the offence of cheating by personation.The complainant, PSI Murkute, said, "I had received the WhatsApp message from an international number and the DP was of Raigad SP Anchal Dalal.The message read, 'I am in a meeting and my mobile is switched off. Immediately transfer Rs 50,000 to my bank account.' I knew the message sender was a scammer. I deliberately replied asking for the bank account number by pretending to send the money. As I received the bank account number from the scammer, it will be useful for the cyber police team to trace the bank account holder. "PSI Murkute added, "One police officer had received a WhatsApp message from the same international number asking to transfer Rs 2,000 by impersonating SP madam and claiming that it was required for filling diesel in the car, and that her mobile battery had drained and she was unable to pay online at the fuel station."API Amol Jadhav of Raigad Cyber Police said, "The cyber scammers use VPNs (Virtual Private Networks) to mask their identity. However, the Internet Protocol (IP) address of the WhatsApp number used by the accused will be obtained to trace the location, and the accused will soon be behind bars."
Article Summary: A cyber fraudster impersonated Raigad SP on WhatsApp, targeting police personnel for money transfers. Fortunately, no one fell prey to the fraud, as the police personnel were aware of this modus operandi used by cyber fraudsters. One police officer received a WhatsApp message from the same international number asking to transfer Rs 2,000 by impersonating SP madam.

Article Title: 3D-printed snake boats bring Onam boat race to school pool
Article Text:
Students of Sree Sarada Vidyalaya, Kalady race remote-controlled snake boats in their swimming pool





Kochi: It was a miniature Nehru Trophy Boat Race in a swimming pool at Sree Sarada Vidyalaya, Kalady, on Friday, as members of the school’s robotics and AI department raced remote-controlled snake boats across the water. Inspired by the iconic Punnamada boat races, the house-wise competition brought together Kerala tradition and student-built technology as part of the school’s Onam celebrations.Tiny snake boats skimmed across the turquoise water of the school’s semi-Olympic pool as cheers rang out from the sidelines. Students leaned over the edge, urging their houses on as sleek, 3D-printed boats darted down their lanes. For a few spirited minutes, the 25-metre pool became a scaled-down Punnamada Lake, complete with house pride, close finishes and an excited crowd.The competition featured four remote-controlled snake boats made of biodegradable plastic, each representing one of the school’s Onam houses — Agni, Akash, Prithvi and Varuna. Varuna emerged the winner.“We conducted a house-wise competition. The students and teachers involved worked together to develop the designs and 3D-print the boats in our robotics lab,” school principal Deepa Chandran said.Emmanuel George, a teacher with the department who coordinated the event, said the idea was to recreate the excitement of Kerala’s famous boat races while encouraging students to apply their engineering and design skills.Each miniaturesnake boat took nearly 24 hours to 3D-print using biodegradable plastic. Powered by a BLDC motor, the boats could reach speeds of up to 40 kmph, adding a dash of engineering precision to the festive race.The principal said the school created projects that bring together culture and emerging technology every year. Previous Onam-themed creations by the department included an automated chenda and a moving Kathakali model with animated eyes.
Article Summary: Students of Sree Sarada Vidyalaya, Kalady, race remote-controlled snake boats in their swimming pool. Inspired by the iconic Punnamada boat races, the house-wise competition brought together Kerala tradition and student-built technology.

Article Title: New York’s $95 million flood plan will turn parks, schoolyards and streets into hidden stormwater storage, an underground defence against extreme rainfall
Article Text:
New York’s Homecrest plan aims to capture stormwater before flooding

The quiet infrastructure designed to hold back heavy rain

The hidden effort to slow down stormwater during heavy rain

How New York is redesigning its response to extreme rainfall

The growing pressure on New York’s ageing drainage network

Protecting Coney Island Creek

Beneath parks, schoolyards, parking areas and other public spaces, New York is planning to create underground storage capable of holding stormwater before it overwhelms the sewer network. According to NYC Gov, the $95 million Homecrest project is part of a wider shift in how the city prepares for increasingly intense rainfall, using everyday public spaces as part of the drainage system rather than relying entirely on pipes and sewers.The project will cover roughly 350 acres around some of the neighbourhood’s most flood-prone streets and is designed for storms that can drop more than two inches of rain in an hour. Above ground, much may look unchanged. But during a sudden downpour, those familiar spaces could quietly become part of a hidden system designed to hold millions of gallons of water back from flooded streets and Coney Island Creek.The plan centres on a simple change in how rainwater is handled. Instead of sending every drop towards the existing sewer network as quickly as possible, some of it will be caught locally and held underground.That matters during short, intense storms, when the volume arriving on streets can rise very quickly. The Homecrest scheme is being designed around downpours capable of delivering more than two inches of rain in an hour. Those events can put considerable strain on drainage infrastructure, particularly in low-lying parts of southern Brooklyn.According to NYC Gov, the city says the project will cover about 350 acres, with work focused on known flooding trouble spots around Kings Highway, Coney Island Avenue and several of the surrounding avenues, including P, R, S, T, U and V.The city is working with its parks, transport and schools departments to identify public sites that can accommodate underground tanks. Traffic triangles, athletic courts, schoolyards and parking areas are among the places being assessed.The idea is to make use of land that already serves the neighbourhood without turning it into a conventional drainage facility. Water can be collected during a storm, stored below ground and dealt with later, after the immediate pressure on the drainage system has eased.Porous pavement forms another part of the scheme. Rather than allowing rain to sheet across an entirely sealed surface, permeable sections can let water move through the pavement and into systems beneath it.For residents, that could mean infrastructure that is easy to overlook on a dry day but performs a very different job when the rain arrives.Reportedly, DEP estimates that the completed Homecrest project will manage about 30 million gallons of stormwater annually.That figure is not the amount of water that will simply disappear. The purpose is to capture and temporarily store runoff so that less reaches the sewer network at the most difficult point of a storm.There is a second concern beyond flooded roads and overloaded drains. Rainwater flowing over streets can pick up oil, rubbish and other pollutants before reaching local waterways. In Homecrest, the project is also intended to reduce the amount of polluted runoff entering Coney Island Creek.New York began its Cloudburst Management Program in 2023, with the same broad principle being tested in several flood-prone neighbourhoods.Projects are under way or being advanced in places including Parkchester in the Bronx, Brownsville and East New York in Brooklyn, East Harlem in Manhattan, and Corona, Jamaica, Kissena and St. Albans in Queens.The approach reflects a shift away from relying solely on traditional underground sewer capacity. New infrastructure can still involve pipes and drains, but the city is also looking at streets, parks and other public land as part of the stormwater system.Homecrest is one of the larger commitments under that programme, with $95 million in DEP funding allocated to the project.The timing of the investment is tied to a practical problem facing the city's drainage network. Short bursts of very heavy rain can overwhelm systems that may cope perfectly well with more moderate rainfall spread over a longer period.The Homecrest project is being designed specifically for those cloudburst conditions. Rather than trying to move all the water away immediately, the system is intended to slow it down and create somewhere for it to go.That approach is particularly relevant in southern Brooklyn, where residents and local officials have repeatedly raised concerns about flooding during major storms. The memory of Hurricane Sandy also remains part of the area's experience with extreme weather.The city has described the investment as part of a broader effort to strengthen neighbourhoods against increasingly intense rainfall while protecting waterways from untreated runoff.Flood management is not the only environmental objective behind the project. During intense rainfall, runoff can move quickly from roads and other hard surfaces into the sewer network or nearby waterways.Capturing some of that water before it reaches those routes can reduce the amount of contaminated runoff entering Coney Island Creek. The city says this will help improve water quality and support its obligations under the federal Clean Water Act.That makes the project less about simply keeping particular streets dry. It is also about controlling what happens to rainwater after it hits the ground.
Article Summary: $95 million Homecrest project is part of a wider shift in how the city prepares for increasingly intense rainfall. Project will cover roughly 350 acres around some of the neighbourhood’s most flood-prone streets. Water can be collected during a storm, stored below ground and dealt with later, after the immediate pressure on the drainage system has eased.

Article Title: Japan installed a 1.1 MW turbine beneath the Naru Strait, using predictable tidal currents to generate clean electricity for the Goto Islands
Article Text:
Image AI generated

How Japan’s 1.1 MW AR1100 tidal turbine generates electricity underwater

Image AI generated

Japan’s tidal energy project grows from a 500 kW pilot to a 1.1 MW turbine

Why predictable tidal energy could complement solar and wind in Japan

The engineering challenges of operating a tidal turbine underwater

Between Japan’s Goto Islands, the sea is doing something that is usually associated with wind farms and solar fields. Beneath the surface of the Naru Strait, a 1.1 MW turbine is drawing energy from water moving with the tides and sending electricity back towards land through a subsea cable. No blades are turning in the sky and no panels spread across the shoreline. The machine works largely out of sight, following currents whose timing can be forecast well in advance. Installed by Proteus Marine Renewables, the AR1100 grew from an earlier 500 kW trial in the same waters. Its deployment has given Japan a megawatt-scale tidal system designed to work with the regular rise and fall of the sea rather than depending on sunshine or changing winds.The project also demonstrates the potential of tidal power in narrow channels, where fast-moving water can provide a concentrated source of renewable energy. By placing the turbine underwater, the system avoids taking up large areas of land while tapping into a resource that follows a predictable natural cycle.Unlike solar and wind power, tidal energy has one major advantage: its timing can be predicted years ahead because tides follow the gravitational pull of the Moon and Sun.That predictability could make tidal turbines useful alongside renewable sources whose output changes with weather conditions.The AR1100 is installed in the Naru Strait near Japan’s Goto Islands. Unlike a conventional wind turbine, there is no tower standing above the water and no set of panels covering land. The generating equipment works underwater, where tidal currents pass through its three-bladed rotor and turn the machinery inside the nacelle. Electricity then travels towards shore through a subsea connection. According to Proteus Marine Renewables, the turbine was deployed in February 2025, while later company information recorded that it received Japanese certification and began exporting electricity to the grid in June 2025.The arrangement is fairly straightforward in principle, although operating it beneath the sea is not. The rotor extracts energy from moving water, the drivetrain passes that mechanical power to a permanent-magnet generator, and the resulting electricity is carried to an onshore station. A yaw system turns the nacelle as the tidal flow reverses, while independently controlled blades can alter their pitch to regulate how the turbine responds to changing conditions. AR1100 is a horizontal-axis turbine mounted on a gravity-based support structure. The earlier project in the same strait provided the starting point for the larger machine.Offshore Energy reported that the earlier 500 kW AR500 pilot operated in the Naru Strait with 97% availability in 2021. That earlier machine had a rated capacity of 500 kW and recorded 97% availability during its operation, according to the material released about the project. The experience allowed engineers to see how the technology behaved in the actual marine environment rather than only in controlled testing.The next version increased the rated capacity to 1.1 MW and introduced changes to the turbine's control systems. An equipment supply and works contract with Kyuden Mirai Energy was signed in November 2022, with the Japanese project subsequently moving towards the upgraded machine. Advanced pitch and yaw systems were incorporated as part of the work. The company says those changes were intended to improve the turbine's performance and efficiency while allowing it to deal more effectively with the changing direction of the tidal flow.The most distinctive feature of tidal power is not simply that the turbines sit underwater. It is the predictability of the resource. Solar output changes with daylight and weather conditions. Wind can strengthen, weaken or stop altogether. ClickPetroleogas noted that tidal production can be estimated in advance because the cycles follow predictable natural patterns, unlike renewable generation that is more affected by weather conditions. The electricity produced at any particular moment still depends on the conditions at the site and the performance of the equipment; the underlying movement of the water is far less of a surprise.That distinction matters when renewable sources are being combined. A grid operator cannot make the sun shine or order the wind to blow, whereas the timing of tidal cycles can be incorporated into generation planning. It does not make tidal energy constant; the flow rises and falls as the tide changes, but it makes the pattern easier to anticipate. For islands such as those around the Goto group, where space and fuel logistics can present particular constraints, a submerged source can sit alongside solar, wind and other forms of generation. The Naru Strait project is intended to contribute to reducing emissions from the islands' electricity supply.Underwater generation creates its own engineering problems. Components have to survive saltwater, strong currents and long periods of exposure while remaining accessible enough for inspection and maintenance. Getting people and equipment to a submerged turbine can also require vessels, specialist crews and careful planning. The location itself has to provide sufficient water movement, suitable depth and a practical route for sending the electricity into the grid.The Naru Strait project therefore depends on more than the turbine turning. Its subsea cable links the machine to an onshore electrical station, where the generated power can be processed for distribution. Local vessels and resources were used during deployment, with Proteus' offshore team overseeing the work, while Kyuden Mirai Energy and Japan's Ministry of Environment have been involved in advancing the project.There is also a useful way to think about the long-term promise of the machine, without treating its output as something that can be guaranteed hour by hour. The tidal timetable itself is highly predictable. Engineers can calculate when stronger and weaker currents are expected well into the future, creating a generation pattern that can be plotted ahead of time. What cannot simply be printed on that chart is the turbine's actual electricity production for every future hour: maintenance, operating conditions and other technical factors still matter.That distinction is important. The Naru Strait turbine is not a giant power station, nor does the available source material establish that it will produce a fixed amount of electricity every hour for a decade. What the project demonstrates is something more specific: a megawatt-scale machine can be installed beneath a Japanese strait, connected to shore and operated using an energy source whose basic timing is known far in advance. The water will keep changing direction. The turbine is built to follow it.
Article Summary: The AR1100 is installed in the Naru Strait near Japan’s Goto Islands. Unlike a conventional wind turbine, there is no tower standing above the water. The generating equipment works underwater, where tidal currents pass through its three-bladed rotor and turn the machinery inside the nacelle. Electricity then travels towards shore through a subsea connection.

Article Title: China’s 16.18-km undersea high-speed rail tunnel completes 21-day cutter replacement under extreme pressure
Article Text:
Image: AI Generated

How China’s Jintang undersea tunnel completed high-pressure shield cutter replacement

Engineers replaced 104 cutting tools under high pressure

The “Deep-Sea Space Station” allows longer work shifts

China is pushing high-speed rail through underwater environments

Deep beneath the waters off eastern China, engineers are carrying out one of the most demanding stages of construction on a high-speed railway tunnel. The Jintang undersea tunnel, part of the Ningbo-Zhoushan high-speed railway in Zhejiang Province, has completed the inspection and replacement of 104 shield cutting tools after 21 days of work under intense water and soil pressure. The 16.18-kilometre tunnel is set to become the world’s longest undersea high-speed rail tunnel, linking Ningbo with Zhoushan and cutting the journey between the two cities from as much as two hours to about 26 minutes. The latest operation also tested a domestically developed saturation hyperbaric system adapted from deep-sea diving technology. The achievement comes as China continues pushing high-speed rail construction through challenging underwater environments, including the recently completed shield-machine crossing beneath the Yangtze River, another major engineering milestone highlighted by China’s State Council Information Office . The operation demonstrates how construction methods are being adapted to underwater conditions safely too.The Jintang tunnel is the critical undersea section of the Ningbo-Zhoushan high-speed railway and stretches 16.18 kilometres, including an 11.21-kilometre shield-bored section. It will connect the port city of Ningbo with the Zhoushan islands, where journeys currently rely heavily on roads and ferries. Once the railway opens, travel between Ningbo and Zhoushan is expected to take as little as 26 minutes, compared with roughly 1.5 to 2 hours today.The tunnel is being excavated from opposite shores using two super-large-diameter shield machines. One machine, Yongzhou, must bore 4,940 metres through 24 alternating layers of soft and hard rock, representing nearly 70 per cent of its route and creating severe wear on its cutting tools. Excavation progress is being monitored carefully. The geological conditions make the project particularly demanding. Rock strength along the route reaches 191 megapascals, placing some of the material in the high-strength to very-high-strength category. As the cutting head moves through alternating rock layers, its tools experience substantial mechanical stress and wear. That made the latest replacement operation necessary, but carrying out such maintenance deep beneath the seabed presented a challenge of its own. At the tunnel’s deepest point, the excavation reaches about 92 metres below sea level, where combined water and soil pressure can reach 8.5 bar. A roughly 2,000-metre section experiences pressure above 6 bar. These conditions mean that workers cannot simply enter the cutting chamber using conventional methods and carry out maintenance as they would in a normal tunnel.The latest operation involved inspecting and replacing 104 shield cutting tools over 21 days. These tools sit at the front of the tunnel-boring machine and are responsible for breaking through the rock and soil ahead of it. Their condition is critical because worn cutters can reduce excavation efficiency and make continued tunnelling more difficult. The operation was carried out under high water pressure, turning what would ordinarily be a demanding mechanical maintenance job into a complex human-safety challenge. Global Times reported that conventional compressed-air methods provide workers with only around 40 minutes of effective working time per person each day and are generally limited to depths of approximately 60 metres. The Jintang tunnel’s deeper and higher-pressure conditions required a different approach. The construction team spent three years adapting technology derived from deep-sea saturation diving. The result was described as China’s first domestically developed saturation hyperbaric system for shield tunnelling, nicknamed the “Deep-Sea Space Station” by the project team. Rather than repeatedly exposing workers to major pressure changes, the system allows them to remain in a controlled pressurised environment for extended periods.The system consists of living, transfer and control modules designed to allow workers to operate safely under the extreme conditions surrounding the tunnel boring machine. The system can accommodate nine workers for extended periods, with crew members travelling to the work face through a transfer chamber. They can work for up to eight hours at a time, allowing round-the-clock multi-shift operations for as long as 28 days. One of the key advantages is that workers undergo a single controlled decompression after completing their assignment instead of repeatedly moving between normal atmospheric pressure and the high-pressure working environment. This reduces the risks associated with frequent pressure changes and makes prolonged underwater construction work more manageable. The technology represents an unusual overlap between offshore engineering and underground construction. Techniques developed for people working at significant depths underwater have been adapted to create a controlled environment inside a tunnel-boring operation. In practical terms, the system gives engineers more time at the cutting face while reducing the number of dangerous pressure transitions workers must endure. The successful 21-day cutter replacement operation therefore represents more than routine maintenance. It provided a real-world test of whether the new system could support prolonged work under the pressure conditions encountered by the Jintang tunnel.The Jintang project forms part of a broader expansion of high-speed rail infrastructure through some of China’s most challenging terrain. The Ningbo-Zhoushan railway is designed to bring Zhoushan more directly into the national high-speed rail network, with the undersea tunnel providing a crucial connection beneath the water separating the islands from mainland Zhejiang. The project also comes shortly after another major underwater railway milestone in China. On July 31, 2026, the State Council Information Office reported that China had completed excavation of the tunnel beneath the Yangtze River for the Shanghai-Chongqing-Chengdu high-speed railway. The project uses the large-diameter shield machine Linghang and is designed for high-speed trains travelling at up to 350 kilometres per hour without slowing for the underwater section.The two projects involve different waterways and engineering challenges, but together they demonstrate the scale of China’s efforts to extend high-speed rail through difficult underwater environments. While the Yangtze project required a record-setting shield machine to pass beneath one of the country’s largest rivers, the Jintang project is tackling prolonged excavation beneath the seabed, where high rock strength and intense pressure complicate both boring and maintenance. For the Jintang tunnel, is also another step towards completing a connection expected to dramatically shorten travel between Ningbo and Zhoushan. The Yongzhou shield machine has already advanced 3,936 metres, or nearly 80 per cent of its assigned task. If construction continues as planned, the finished tunnel will not simply provide a faster route between two cities. It will also stand as a demonstration of how large-scale rail infrastructure can be built in environments where conventional tunnelling techniques reach their limits, with workers and machines operating beneath some of the most challenging pressure conditions encountered in modern rail construction.
Article Summary: Engineers replaced 104 cutting tools under high pressure. The Jintang undersea tunnel is part of the Ningbo-Zhoushan high-speed railway in Zhejiang Province. The 16.18-kilometre tunnel is set to become the world’s longest undersea high- speed rail tunnel.

Article Title: Canada lowered a retired Boeing 737 onto the seabed off Vancouver Island; the 100-foot jet now sits nearly 90 feet underwater as an artificial reef for marine life
Article Text:
A jet to a reef

Xihuw, is the Hul'qumi'num word for the red sea urchins that used to live in abundance in these waters

Life in a jet

Cloud sponges, plumose anemones, feather stars, octopuses, and the site's namesake red sea urchins have all colonised the aircraft's surfaces over the years.

A Boeing 737 aircraft that was originally the part of the Canadian Airlines fleet now lies nearly 90 feet underwater and serves the role of an artificial reef for marine life. The 100-foot jet was decommissioned by Air Canada due to age and structural problems, stripped of all usable components and the airframe was donated to the ARSBC. It was sunk by the ARSBC near Chemainus, BC on January 14, 2006.Now known as Xihuw, it was donated by Qwest Airparts of Memphis, Tennessee, through the efforts of Air Canada. Xihuw, is the Hul'qumi'num word for the red sea urchins that used to live in abundance in these waters but whose population has dwindled, sadly, due to pollution and over-fishing. The first step began with a phone call from Fraser MacLean of Air Canada in November 2002. The company had a Boeing 737 that was slated to be decommissioned. Fraser had seen the coverage of the HMCS Cape Breton’s sinking, and thought the ARSBC might be interested in acquiring the Boeing 737 for its second reef.The plane, which had been stripped down, weighs 15 tonnes and measures 30 metres long. The process of finding an underwater home for the aircraft proved a turbulent one, with sites considered from Vancouver to Sechelt to Courtenay/Comox and Victoria.Southern Vancouver island became the final home thanks to the community support garnered by Peter Luckham of 49th Parallel Diving.Volunteers spent hundreds of hours scrubbing the fuselage clean of grease, insulation, and any residual pollutants, ensuring nothing toxic would leach into the marine environment once it was underwater. After nearly four years of planning, including securing approval from Environment Canada and six local First Nations, the project was cleared for its final descent. On Saturday January 14, 2006, the plane was mounted on 11-foot-high support stands and lowered by crane into the waters of Georgia Strait off Chemainus.Cranes slowly lowered the decommissioned plane into the ocean off Chemainus, about 70 kilometres north of Victoria, slightly more than a month after Environment Canada gave final approval to a plan dreamed up by diving fans. The site was chosen specifically because the region lacked significant marine life at the time, having been affected by decades of forest-industry debris on the seafloor. The plane was mounted on stands about 11 feet high, positioned so divers could swim not just through the cabin, but underneath the fuselage as well. The sinking was documented for the Discovery Channel series Mega Builders.Within a few years, the ARSBC's projections of new sea life proved accurate, and today the wreck hosts more than a hundred documented species. Rockfish shelter along the wings and fuselage, lingcod rest on the surrounding sand, and schools of juvenile fish use the plane's structure for cover. Cloud sponges, plumose anemones, feather stars, octopuses, and the site's namesake red sea urchins have all colonised the aircraft's surfaces over the years.Today, the Xihwu Reef sits at a maximum depth of about 90 feet, with the fuselage itself around 70 feet down — well within recreational diving limits, though cold water and current mean a thick wetsuit or drysuit is essential. Divers can enter the cabin, now stripped of seats, and look down through openings into the old cargo holds, or make their way forward to the cockpit, where small rockfish frequently gather. A memorial plaque honouring two WWII pilots, along with a carved wooden mask that once adorned the aircraft's nose, is mounted on one of the support stands.Local dive charters regularly take visitors to the site from Chemainus, and the wreck has become one of the popular dive sites on Vancouver Island. Nearly 20 years after it was placed underwater, the 737 has taken on a new role, serving as an artificial reef and providing a habitat for marine life.
Article Summary: Xihuw, is the Hul'qumi'num word for the red sea urchins that used to live in abundance in these waters but whose population has dwindled, sadly, due to pollution and over-fishing. The 100-foot jet was decommissioned by Air Canada due to age and structural problems, stripped of all usable components and the airframe was donated to the ARSBC.

Article Title: Meet the Humanoid Robot winning hearts in China after running 100 meter in less than 10 seconds; faster than any men's world record
Article Text:
Image courtesy: South China Morning Post

Rivalry with Honor’s lightning

Strategic industry for China

Global participation

A Chinese humanoid robot named Tiangong Ultra has captured global attention after running 100 metres in 9.39 seconds, faster than Usain Bolt’s men’s world record of 9.58 seconds, according to a report by Reuters. Developed by the Beijing Humanoid Robot Innovation Center, Tiangong Ultra won its preliminary heat at the second edition of the World Humanoid Robot Games in Beijing, overtaking rival robot Lightning near the finish line.Lightning, built by smartphone maker Honor, finished close behind in 9.47 seconds, also faster than Bolt’s record set at the 2009 World Athletics Championships in Berlin. Earlier tests showed Lightning clocking 9.32 seconds, reaching a peak speed of 14.5 metres per second. Despite their speed, both robots lacked Bolt’s finesse — Tiangong stumbled into the sidelines, while Lightning collapsed and had to be carried away on a stretcher.Rapid progress since last yearThe results mark a dramatic leap from last year’s inaugural games, when Tiangong Ultra won the 100m in 21.50 seconds. Tiangong also made history by winning the world’s first humanoid half‑marathon in Beijing in 2025. Lightning, meanwhile, claimed this year’s half‑marathon title in 50 minutes and 26 seconds, faster than the pace of the elite men’s human world record.The 100m sprint is one of 51 events at the games, which also feature football, dancing, and industrial‑task contests. China has designated humanoid robots as a strategic emerging industry, betting that advances in AI and hardware will accelerate their adoption in manufacturing, logistics, and consumer applications. Investor enthusiasm is evident: shares of Unitree, China’s best‑known humanoid robot maker, surged more than fivefold in their Shanghai debut this week, giving the company a market value of about $50 billion.This year’s games, held at Beijing’s National Speed Skating Oval, have drawn 2,056 robots from 666 teams across 16 countries and six continents, a sharp increase from 280 teams last year.
Article Summary: Tiangong Ultra ran 100m in 9.39 seconds, faster than Usain Bolt’s world record of 9.58 seconds. It overtook rival robot Lightning, built by smartphone maker Honor, in the final. China has designated humanoid robots as a strategic emerging industry, betting that advances in AI will accelerate their adoption.

Article Title: Meet Peter Fernández Dulay, the Florida eighth-grader who asked four AI generators what scientists look like; only 17.4% of the images showed women alone
Article Text:
The idea came about when Peter and his younger sister Elisa were using the Magic Media AI tool by Canva. (Images: istock and Society for Science)

A simple question with bigger implications

Testing 4 AI image generators

Not all AI tools are created equally

Fencing to robots

Envisioning a more inclusive AI

Peter Fernández Dulay’s younger sister asked an AI tool to draw a scientist and hoped to see someone who looked like the scientists she might be one day. The pictures, however, showed the same figure again and again: an older man with light skin and gray, frizzy hair. According to Society for Science data, that simple observation sparked Peter, an eighth-grader from Florida, to launch a research project on how artificial intelligence represents people in science and technology. His findings posed a troubling question: If AI learns from existing data that contains stereotypes, does the technology reproduce those same biases? Scroll down to know what exactly happened.The idea came about when Peter and his younger sister Elisa were using the Magic Media AI tool by Canva. Elisa was writing a story about a mad scientist and she needed an image to go with it. But the results took her by surprise. The images mostly featured older, light-skinned men, rather than producing a wide diversity of scientists. Seeing his sister’s dismay, Peter started to wonder if the pattern was limited to one AI tool. According to the project background, women make up about 35 percent of STEM graduates. Peter wanted to see if AI image generators would show women in science at anything like that proportion.Peter tried out four popular AI image-generating platforms: Shutterstock, Canva, DALL-E and Midjourney. Rather than request images of scientists in general, he chose five specific careers in science and technology: actuary, data scientist, information security analyst, operations research analyst and computer and information research scientist. The tools produced several image sets for each prompt. Peter then viewed and coded the images for whether they depicted men or women. The results demonstrated a large gender imbalance across the entire experiment. According to the report, he analyzed 1,459 images of men and 347 images of women. Women alone accounted for only 17.4 percent of the images. The only one of the five career prompts where women’s representation in the results was at least as high as the percentage of women in that field was information security analyst.Peter’s experiment also showed differences between the platforms. His analysis found that of the four tools he tested, Shutterstock yielded the least biased results, while Midjourney was the most biased. But the findings don’t necessarily mean that an AI system is biased on purpose. AI image generators are trained on patterns learned from huge swathes of existing material – and those swathes can contain historic inequalities and stereotypes. But when these patterns are repeated over and over again, they can shape the way people think about certain careers. That may be important to a young student like Elisa. If the default image of a scientist is always an older man, kids may absorb the idea that science belongs to people who look like that, without even realizing it.But Peter’s interests go far beyond AI research. He is a regionally ranked fencer and on his school’s robotics team. He calls fencing "physical chess," a sport that demands quick decisions and a close analysis of an opponent, the report by Society for Science states. Fencing has taught him how to deal with stress, and robotics lets him explore his technical interests, he says in the post. His range of interests may also explain why he is thinking about technology through a human lens.Peter would like to become a psychologist, and he has an idea of how AI could someday fit into that career. He is bilingual and multicultural and he sees the creation of an AI companion that can speak to people in different languages and can also recognize psychological stress via language patterns. For now, his research offers a useful lesson about artificial intelligence: technology does not exist separate from the information used to create it.
Article Summary: Peter Fernández Dulay, an eighth-grader from Florida, tried out four popular AI image-generating platforms: Shutterstock, Canva, DALL-E and Midjourney. The results demonstrated a large gender imbalance across the entire experiment. Women alone accounted for only 17.4 percent of the images.

Article Title: In 1988, a Texas man began wiring discarded objects together behind his small home; decades later, more than 60 tons of junk had become a walk-through cathedral
Article Text:
The Cathedral of Junk in Austin, Texas, created by Vince Hannemann, transforms discarded everyday objects into an ever-growing maze of art, architecture and found-object history. Image Credits: Lorie Shaull/Flickr

From backyard pile to cathedral

When junk met the city

Vince Hannemann's backyard folk art environment built out of cast-offs, dross, and debris. Image Credits: Wikimedia Commons.

A living piece of outsider art

A broken bicycle, an old television, a shopping trolley and a collection of battered signs might seem destined for a scrapyard. In a South Austin backyard, however, thousands of such objects became something altogether different. For decades, artist Vince Hannemann has been wiring, stacking and fitting discarded objects together to create the Cathedral of Junk, a three-storey maze of towers, arches, rooms and walkways that is now one of the city’s most unusual landmarks.What began as Hannemann’s personal backyard experiment gradually became a project shaped by the wider neighbourhood. As the structure grew, neighbours began bringing him unwanted possessions they thought could be incorporated into it. Over time, the supply of material became so abundant that Hannemann no longer had to search for much of it himself. People simply turned up with objects they believed might find a place in the expanding maze of towers, arches and passageways. By the 2010s, the cathedral was estimated to contain about 60 tons of discarded material.The early structure was far less elaborate than the one visitors see today.Hannemann gradually connected pieces of metal, household objects, bicycle parts, car components, signs and other cast-offs, using wire and other fasteners to hold the growing construction together. There was no conventional architectural blueprint. Instead, the cathedral developed through accumulation. One object suggested another, and new sections were added around existing ones. The result was less a conventional building than a continually evolving installation.The structure eventually reached roughly 30 feet in height and developed multiple rooms, narrow passages, bridges, stairways and towers. Objects that would normally be separated by function or era became part of the same visual landscape. Old appliances sit beside toys, bicycle wheels and licence plates, while arches and openings turn what could have been an enormous heap into something visitors can actually walk through.According to a study in Arts and Design Studies , artists can transform discarded materials into aesthetic works by shifting them from their original context and giving them new creative purposes. The study notes that waste and found objects can become alternative artistic materials rather than simply being treated as unwanted objects. The Cathedral of Junk takes this approach beyond an individual artwork, turning thousands of discarded objects into a walk-through environment.As the Cathedral grew, its unusual scale eventually attracted attention in the surrounding residential neighbourhood. Although much of the structure stood behind the house and trees rather than directly along the street, its height and sprawling form made it visible from neighbouring properties. In 2010, a complaint prompted Austin officials to inspect the structure, raising concerns about electrical wiring, access and other safety issues. Engineers examined the construction, and Hannemann began making changes to meet the city’s requirements. The dispute became serious enough that demolition appeared possible. In June 2010, Hannemann briefly began dismantling parts of the Cathedral, arguing that the changes required by the city were altering too much of the work’s character. He later reconsidered, and an agreement allowed the Cathedral to remain under certain restrictions. Some parts of the installation had to be removed, including material that extended into the property’s setback, but the central structure was preserved.Unlike a conventional sculpture meant to remain fixed, the Cathedral of Junk grew through the continual addition and rearrangement of discarded objects. This approach also places Hannemann’s work within the broader tradition of junk and found-object art. A study in ShodhKosh: Journal of Visual and Performing Arts traces how artists have used discarded and industrial materials to create new forms of art, giving ordinary objects new contexts and meanings. This connection helps explain what makes the Cathedral distinctive: its materials are not hidden or merely used as structural elements. Old bicycles, car parts, signs, household objects and other discarded items remain recognisable, allowing their previous identities to become part of the artwork while contributing to the constantly changing character of the structure.The Cathedral of Junk is an artwork that visitors experience from within rather than simply view from a distance. Its narrow passages, rooms and towers encourage people to move through the structure, discovering objects and details from different angles and heights. Over the years, it has also hosted weddings, parties and other gatherings, adding a social dimension to the installation. What began as a personal collection of discarded objects gradually became a place that invites visitors to reconsider the boundary between waste and art. For Hannemann, that transformation did not happen all at once. It took shape over decades, as each new object found a place within the growing structure.
Article Summary: Vince Hannemann's Cathedral of Junk is a three-storey maze of towers, arches, rooms and walkways that is now one of the city’s most unusual landmarks. As the structure grew, neighbours began bringing him unwanted possessions they thought could be incorporated into it. By the 2010s the cathedral was estimated to contain about 60 tons of discarded material.

Article Title: Meet Frank Lucci, the 18-year-old Texas student who built a high-precision robot sensor for under $25; it is nearly 20 times cheaper than existing options
Article Text:
Born in San Antonio, Lucci built SubArc for his engineering project for the Regeneron Science Talent Search.

A sensor designed to make robotics more accessible

Precision without the price

A young inventor who’s eyes are on space

Lucci's engineering interests extend far beyond SubArc. He is a student at BASIS San Antonio Shavano, where he founded his school’s aerospace club and is a founding member of its robotics team, adds the online report.

A tiny sensor with huge potential

Outside the lab

Imagine building a tiny piece of technology that tells robots exactly how they are moving, and doing it for the cost of a typical dinner. This is exactly what 18-year-old Texas student Frank Lucci set out to do with SubArc, an innovative high-resolution sensor designed to make precision robotics more affordable and accessible, reports Society for Science. Scroll down to read the details about his innovation.Born in San Antonio, Lucci built SubArc for his engineering project for the Regeneron Science Talent Search. He’s built a high-resolution rotary encoder, a device that converts mechanical motion into digital signals so that machines can accurately record rotation and position, explains an online report published by the Society for Science website. For the uninitiated, rotary encoders are essential parts of robotics, but high-resolution models can cost hundreds or even thousands of dollars. That price can be prohibitive for independent researchers, student teams and programs with limited budgets, working with advanced robotics technology, that was something Lucci was determined to change.The website states that SubArc uses magnets to measure rotation with a lot of precision. The design is also intended to be reliable in dusty environments, an important benefit for robots working outside the traditional laboratory.And Lucci’s big innovation was finding a new way to handle the signal from the sensor. This allowed him to lower the cost of parts and simplify the manufacturing process while maintaining the resolution of the sensor. The outcome is a small, open-source, customizable device that costs under $25— nearly 20 times less than similar existing options. Instead of beginning with a large and expensive prototype, Lucci took another approach. He began by designing smaller versions, building a system that could be scaled up eventually. This strategy allowed him to obtain high precision with low manufacturing costs.Lucci's engineering interests extend far beyond SubArc. He is a student at BASIS San Antonio Shavano, where he founded his school’s aerospace club and is a founding member of its robotics team, adds the online report. He is also a cross country runner, balancing athletics with an ambitious interest in science and engineering.His experience has also led him beyond the classroom. Lucci first volunteered at Astroport Space Technologies, a lunar construction company, and then interned there. While working for the company he helped develop a robotic frame to maneuver a device that could make bricks from lunar soil, and that experience connects his work on affordable robotics to an even larger challenge: building machines that can work in the harsh and demanding environment of space.SubArc proves that you don’t need a huge budget to do groundbreaking engineering. By re-thinking the sensor's design, and how to process its signals, Lucci has opened up a potentially more accessible path to high-precision robotics. If open-source technology like SubArc can provide researchers and students with precision sensors at a fraction of the traditional cost, it may encourage more people to experiment, build and innovate, adds the online report.But Lucci’s hobby is surprisingly stylish; he collects promotional sunglasses frames, apart from robotics and aerospace. He has more than 30 frames in his collection and gets prescription lenses custom-cut to match their shapes. That means he can change styles whenever he wants. Lucci’s interests may be diverse—from lunar construction robots to a collection of sunglasses—but his work on SubArc shows a clear talent for turning ambitious ideas into practical inventions.Images Courtesy: istock and Society for Science
Article Summary: 18-year-old Frank Lucci built SubArc for his engineering project for the Regeneron Science Talent Search. He’s built a high-resolution rotary encoder, a device that converts mechanical motion into digital signals so that machines can accurately record rotation and position. The outcome is a small, open-source, customizable device that costs under $25.

Article Title: In the early 1970s, Virginia Beach compacted 640,000 tons of garbage into a 60-foot hill; the dump became America’s first landfill park and now spans 165 acres
Article Text:
Mount Trashmore Park (Image Credit: Wikipedia)

Turning waste into a hill

A 165-acre transformation

Trails around the mountain

A space for families

More than a covered landfill

From garbage to public space

In Virginia Beach, one of the city's most recognisable parks began with something most communities would rather hide: a mountain of garbage. According to the City of Virginia Beach, a 640,000-ton pile of garbage was converted into a 60-foot-high hill that became Mount Trashmore Park. What had once been a landfill was transformed into a 165-acre public space with lakes, trails, playgrounds and recreational facilities. The City of Virginia Beach describes Mount Trashmore as the nation's first landfill park. The unusual project began in the early 1970s and demonstrated how land associated with waste could be given an entirely different purpose. Today, visitors can climb the artificial mountain, walk around its lakes, use the park's trails and spend time in green spaces without necessarily realising that the landscape beneath them was once a landfill.Mount Trashmore was created during a period when Virginia Beach needed a solution for handling large quantities of municipal waste. Instead of leaving the landfill as an abandoned dumping ground, the city developed a plan to reshape it. The garbage was compacted and covered with soil, allowing the material to form a large artificial hill. The resulting mound became Mount Trashmore, rising about 60 feet above the surrounding landscape.The project was not simply an effort to conceal an old landfill. The site was deliberately redesigned as a public recreation area, creating a new use for land previously devoted to waste disposal. The city converted the landfill into a public recreation area, and Mount Trashmore Park opened in 1973. Its transformation made the site an unusual example of landfill reclamation and gave the city a large area of recreational land.Mount Trashmore Park today covers approximately 165 acres. Its most recognisable feature remains the main mountain, but the park has grown into a much larger landscape containing water, greenery and recreational facilities. The park includes two man-made lakes: Lake Trashmore and Lake Windsor. Lake Trashmore is a freshwater lake, while Lake Windsor is a brackish-water lake connected to Thalia Creek.These lakes are now part of the park's recreational environment rather than being associated with its former use as a landfill. Fishing is permitted from land at Lake Trashmore, subject to Virginia's fishing regulations. Kayaks are permitted at Lake Windsor, while boats, swimming and wading are not allowed in the lakes.The artificial mountain is also designed for recreation. Visitors can walk or exercise along trails that pass through different parts of the park. The park also has walking trails that take visitors around the mountain, lakes and surrounding landscape.The main mountain is not the only elevated feature. The park also contains a smaller mound called Encore Hill, adding another distinctive element to the landscape. What makes these features unusual is their origin. Instead of being naturally formed hills, they are part of a landscape created through the redevelopment of a former waste site.Mount Trashmore has also become a destination for families. One of its major attractions is Kids Cove Playground, a large play area designed for children of all abilities. The playground covers nearly 26,000 square feet and includes climbing structures, slides, elevated walkways and swings. According to the City of Virginia Beach, the playground includes a wheelchair swing.Elsewhere in the park, visitors can find areas for skating and BMX riding, along with open spaces suitable for picnics and outdoor activities. The combination of trails, playgrounds, lakes and recreational facilities has helped turn the former landfill into an everyday community space.The transformation of Mount Trashmore is significant because the city did more than close an old dump and cover it with soil. The landfill became the foundation for a carefully planned public landscape. The park also includes environmental features such as a water-wise garden that uses xeriscaping, a landscaping method intended to reduce the need for irrigation.The result is a landscape where the history of the site is largely hidden beneath recreational spaces. Visitors see grass-covered slopes, lakes, trees and playgrounds rather than the landfill that once occupied the area.Mount Trashmore's history illustrates how former waste sites can potentially be repurposed when redevelopment, environmental management and public recreation are brought together. The project also explains why the park's name has endured. Mount Trashmore is a playful reference to its unusual origin, but the site represents a substantial transformation: approximately 640,000 tons of garbage were compacted into an artificial hill that became part of a 165-acre public park.Today, people come to Mount Trashmore to walk, play, exercise, fish, picnic and enjoy the outdoors. Few modern park landscapes make their history quite so obvious in their name. What began as a waste disposal problem eventually became one of Virginia Beach's best-known recreational spaces, a landfill that was given a second life as a park. More than five decades after it opened, Mount Trashmore remains a striking example of how an unlikely piece of land can be transformed into a space for recreation, community and everyday life.
Article Summary: The City of Virginia Beach converted a 640,000-ton pile of garbage into Mount Trashmore Park in the early 1970s. The landfill was compacted and covered with soil to form a 60-foot-high artificial mountain. The city converted the landfill into a 165-acre public space with lakes, trails, playgrounds and recreational facilities. The park opened in 1973 and has become a popular destination for families.

Article Title: Flock CEO says privacy can't be the only priority; it is about safety, as Americans vandalize AI surveillance traffic cameras across US
Article Text:
Flock CEO defends his AI surveillance tool and says privacy can't be the only priority; it's about safety also.

What are Flock cameras?

Tracking but for the wrong reasons

Amid intense backlash over Flock surveillance cameras across America, Flock CEO Garrett Langeley told Fox News that privacy is not the only priority. “I think these are important conversations to have,” he told Saturday in America co-host Kayleigh McEnany, after she asked about the privacy concerns. “I value my privacy… but what we’re talking about is safety as well. And so I think when people talk about just one of these things, privacy or safety, they’re prioritizing the wrong thing. What we have to prioritize as a country is compromise: how do we have our safety, and how do we balance privacy?”Langeley said the call to ban the technology is absurd but there should be regulations. “That’s like banning vehicles. That would never have made sense,” Langley said about a ban. “Instead what we did is we introduced laws against drunk driving, laws around airbags.”It is a surveillance camera system that records and analyses everything that comes in front of it. The company sells its services as a crime-fighting tool and some law enforcement agencies have contracts with Flock to use the cameras' automated license plate readers.Flock has 120,000 automated license plate readers and pan-tilt-zoom cameras throughout the US, which capture billions of data points each month.Flock's ALPRs automatically scan the license plates that pass them, while PTZs record live footage that can be reviewed and analyzed.Flock has been making headlines for all the wrong reasons and police has been caught using the system to stalk exes and colleagues, though the company claimed that the cameras can't track people and they can only log vehicles.Dozens of Flock cameras have been forcibly destroyed in recent weeks. In June, a West Virginia man accused of destroying several Flock cameras was arrested.At least 56 municipalities have deactivated, canceled or rejected contracts with Flock this year, according to national advocacy organization DeFlock. The company announced changes aimed at addressing concerns about privacy and misuse. Flock introduced updated policies around auditing, as well as data retention and sharing – although many critics calling for change consider them inadequate.
Article Summary: Flock has 120,000 automated license plate readers and pan-tilt-zoom cameras throughout the US, which capture billions of data points each month. The company sells its services as a crime-fighting tool and some law enforcement agencies have contracts with Flock.

Article Title: Meet Zeynep Demirbas, the New York eighth-grader who tested whether AI can recognise stress; a basic machine-learning model beat ChatGPT-4o
Article Text:
Zeynep's work earned her a finalist place in the 2025 Thermo Fisher Scientific Junior Innovators Challenge

Testing AI models

What results mean

Zeynep wants to study AI bias

Fourteen-year-old Zeynep Demirbas has found that ChatGPT-4o is less accurate than a mental health-focused AI model and a simpler machine-learning system at detecting stress in human written text.Zeynep, an eighth-grade student at Transit Middle School in East Amherst, New York, tested four different models using more than 3,500 Reddit posts. According to Society for Science, the posts had already been labelled by humans as showing stress or no stress.Her project, titled “ Evaluating the reliability of Large Language Models for stress detection ”, has earned her a place among the finalists in the 2025 Thermo Fisher Scientific Junior Innovators Challenge. The competition recognises young students working on science-based projects.Zeynep became interested in the project after speaking with a family friend who is a psychologist. The psychologist told her that some health insurance companies were exploring large language models (LLMs) as cheaper, 24/7 alternatives to human therapists. Zeynep wondered whether AI systems could actually be trusted to identify stress.To test the models, Zeynep used a dataset called Dreaddit. It contains 3,553 Reddit posts that human raters had labelled according to whether they contained signs of stress.She gave the data to four different models including Bidirectional Encoder Representations from Transformers (BERT), MentalBERT, Random Forest and ChatGPT-4o. MentalBERT is a version of BERT designed for mental health-related language, while Random Forest is a basic machine-learning technique that uses multiple decision trees to make predictions.Zeynep asked each model to identify which posts showed stress. She then used a measure called an F1-score to compare their performance. The score considers both how accurately a model identifies stress and how often it misses stress or wrongly labels a post as showing stress.MentalBERT performed the best in her testing, with a score of about 82 percent. BERT followed with about 79 percent. ChatGPT-4o scored about 74 percent. It also performed worse than the Random Forest model, which was included as a simpler baseline for comparison.The result surprised Zeynep because Random Forest is a much simpler machine-learning method and does not understand language and context in the same way an LLM does. “ChatGPT performing badly was ‘really surprising,’” Zeynep said.She found it particularly interesting that a simpler model could outperform an LLM with millions of parameters. “Random-forest is ‘supposed to be a very simple and old technique. So I just put it in as a baseline,’” Zeynep said, as quoted by Science News Explores. “That was very interesting; how something so small and simple was able to beat an LLM like ChatGPT that used millions of parameters and had so much coding go into it,” she added.Zeynep's findings made her question whether general-purpose LLMs are reliable enough to be used for mental health assessment. A large language model is a type of machine-learning system trained on very large amounts of text. It learns patterns in language and uses them to produce responses.Her results led her to conclude that LLMs should not replace human therapists.“My project shows that LLMs are currently unreliable and unsafe to deploy as diagnostic tools,” Zeynep said.She added that the findings did not mean that LLMs are bad or cannot be useful. But, they show that general-purpose AI systems may not be suitable for a task as sensitive as assessing mental health.“We should be mindful with AI, because it doesn’t really have an acceptable grade in mental health,” Zeynep said. “That doesn’t mean that LLMs are bad, because they’re for general use. They’re not necessarily meant for mental health,” she added.Zeynep also suggested that LLMs could potentially have a different role. Instead of replacing mental health professionals, they might help identify people who are struggling and refer them to a mental health professional.The project also made Zeynep interested in whether LLMs might show different results depending on a person's gender. “One way I feel I could expand it is seeing whether LLMs carry biases toward different genders,” Zeynep said.She said she had read about cases where doctors dismiss symptoms reported by female patients because they believe women are exaggerating. She sees this as an example of personal bias and wants to know whether AI systems could show similar patterns.Since LLMs are trained using large amounts of text created by people, Zeynep believes they can also pick up human biases.Zeynep's work earned her a finalist place in the 2025 Thermo Fisher Scientific Junior Innovators Challenge. She hopes to become a computer scientist.She said she enjoys programming but is particularly interested in how computer science can be applied to real-world problems.
Article Summary: Zeynep Demirbas, an eighth-grade student at Transit Middle School in East Amherst, New York, tested four different models using more than 3,500 Reddit posts. She found that ChatGPT-4o is less accurate than a mental health-focused AI model and a simpler machine-learning system at detecting stress in human written text.
